title: The older, the wiser

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The National Rural Electric Co-operative Association (NRECA) in the state of Virginia in the United States may not be a household name, but in its own humble way it is helping to shape the future. It is a pioneer in coping with one of the biggest challenges facing business: managing older workers. It lets employees work flexible hours and telecommute up to three days a week. It gives them health checks and advice on managing stress, and regularly has ceremonies to congratulate long-serving staff. More than a third of its workers are over 50 and the average employee has been with the company almost 12 years.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Employers often have no choice but to learn how to deal with an ageing workforce, as the baby-boom generation (those born in the years 1946 to 1961) gets older, and life expectancies increase. Yet many are wary of the changes. The Sloan Center on Ageing and Work, at Boston College in the United States, found in a survey that 40% of employers worry that the ageing of the workforce will have a negative or very negative impact on their business. A recent survey by two British management institutes found that only 14% of managers think that their workplaces are prepared to cope with the greying of the workforce.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Peter Cappelli and Bill Novelli delivered a powerful counter-argument to such pessimism in a recent book, Managing the Older Worker. Not only do older workers nowadays want to keep on working, they bring all sorts of benefits. They possess decades' worth of formal and informal knowledge, which risks being lost as the baby-boomers retire, creating an epidemic of skills shortages in aerospace, energy and health care. More often than not, they are the repositories of a company's core values.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: But don't older people bring lots of problems, too? Difficult-to-manage older people are often a source of amusement in film and on television. However, today's elderly are in far better shape than those of earlier generations. There is no doubt that people's muscles do weaken with age, but few jobs require brute force these days: in America 46% of jobs make almost no physical demands on workers, according to the Urban Institute, a think-tank which researches and tries to deal with social policy issues. Although a proportion of older staff are less enthusiastic in embracing ever-changing technology, they make up for it in different ways. Studies suggest that older workers are better at jobs that require personal skills, and a growing proportion of jobs fall into that category. Employers may be mistaken if they assume that older workers lack the vitality to make a go of new ventures. A recent study by the Kauffman Foundation, a research body in the United States, found that Americans aged 55-64 have launched more businesses than those aged 20-34 in every year since 1996. Conscientiousness also tends to rise with age: older workers are less likely to be absent than younger colleagues.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: None of this means that adjusting to an ageing workforce will be easy. Companies will need to rethink the traditional career ladder that linked seniority to pay and power. This is proving easier in the US, where people change jobs more often. But it still has a long way to go in other parts of the world where people tend to cling to their jobs, as well as in hierarchical societies. The biggest barrier to change is psychological: young high-flyers find it hard to tell older workers what to do, and older staff may resent being bossed about by younger employees. Almost 90% of employers worry about hiring older workers because of possible conflicts. Companies need to think harder about training high-flyers to manage their seniors. America's armed forces are ahead of the game here, and already have programmes to teach cadet officers how to work with older sergeants.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Companies also need to think harder about providing satisfying careers for older workers. Several techniques are already proving successful. For example, one Australian bank has asked more experienced workers to act as mentors to less experienced staff. Another technique is to recognise that experienced staff may respond to different incentives: they may be less interested in money and promotion and more concerned with flexibility. Yet another is to treat retirement as a process rather than a sudden event. Some employers offer older workers 'bridge jobs' between full-time work and retirement, such as seasonal jobs that allow them to take long periods of leave without losing their benefits. They are also treating recently retired staff as a just-in-time workforce that can be used to cope with surges in demand, or to fill in for absent colleagues. Examples of this include re-employing retired workers to teach new recruits about the company, or asking retired executives to guide younger managers.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The nightmare that concerns many companies is that older workers spell rigidity. They will trap companies in the past and prevent them from riding the next wave of innovation. But this will be a problem only if companies let it be. Businesses cannot change long-term demographic trends, but they can change the way that they cope with those trends. If they refuse to rethink their standard practices, they might easily see the ageing workforce becoming a trap; but if they rethink those practices, as some companies have done, they could turn older workers into the very model of a modern workforce.
